topic: US Supreme Court Blocks Trump's IEEPA Tariffs

subtopics.title: IEEPA: Origin and Emergency Powers
subtopics.summary: The International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) was enacted in 1977 by President Jimmy Carter to replace the Trading with Enemy Act of 1917. It is primarily a sanctions tool and not a general tariff law. The President can use it only after formally declaring a National Emergency over an unusual and extraordinary threat originating outside the United States.
facts: Enacted in 1977 by President Jimmy Carter
Replaced the Trading with Enemy Act (1917)
Primarily a sanctions tool, not a general tariff law
President must formally declare a National Emergency first
Threat must originate outside the United States
Can freeze foreign assets held in the US
Can block trade with specific countries, entities or individuals
77 national emergencies declared under IEEPA; 46 ongoing as of Sept 2025

subtopics.title: Supreme Court Verdict on IEEPA Tariffs
subtopics.summary: The Supreme Court struck down President Trump's IEEPA tariffs by a 6-3 verdict. Chief Justice John Roberts held that IEEPA does not allow unilateral tariff actions without Congressional approval. The ruling invalidated the Liberation Day tariffs and raised questions about refunds of tariffs already collected.
facts: Verdict: 6-3 against Trump's IEEPA tariffs
Chief Justice John Roberts clarified the Court's reasoning
'Regulate' under IEEPA does not mean 'Tax'
IEEPA cannot serve as broad authority for imposing tariffs
Any such measures require Congressional authorisation
Liberation Day tariffs (executive order of 02 April 2025) invalidated
Ruling raises questions on refunds of previously collected tariffs
Majority: Roberts, Gorsuch, Barrett, Sotomayor, Kagan, Jackson
Dissent: Thomas, Alito, Kavanaugh

subtopics.title: Alternative Tariff Laws After the Ruling
subtopics.summary: The booklet lists several statutes as legal alternatives to IEEPA for imposing tariffs. Section 122 of the Trade Act 1974 allows temporary tariffs, and the President used it to impose a 10% temporary tariff on goods from all countries. Other options are Section 338 of the Tariff Act 1930, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act 1962 and Section 301 of the Trade Act 1974.
facts: Section 122, Trade Act 1974: temporary tariffs up to 15% for up to 150 days
Section 122 aims to protect domestic industries and address trade imbalances
10% temporary tariff imposed on goods from all countries under Section 122
Section 338, Tariff Act 1930: import tariffs up to 50%
Section 338 targets countries with discriminatory trade practices
Section 232, Trade Expansion Act 1962: import restrictions on goods threatening national security
Section 232 has been applied to steel and aluminium
Section 301, Trade Act 1974: action against foreign regulations that unfairly burden US trade

subtopics.title: India's Impact and the 2026 Trade Deal
subtopics.summary: The rollback of Liberation Day tariffs benefits nearly 55% of India's exports to the US, which had faced an 18% levy. These goods now face only standard Most-Favoured Nation (MFN) tariff rates, while Section 232 duties remain in force. The 2026 India-US trade deal includes Indian commitments on energy, technology and agricultural trade.
facts: Nearly 55% of India's exports to the US benefit from the rollback
Those goods previously faced an 18% levy
Benefiting goods are now subject only to standard MFN tariff rates
Section 232 tariffs of 50% on steel and aluminium remain in force
25% Section 232 tariff on select automotive components remains in force
25% penalty for purchasing Russian oil has been eliminated
India commits to massive procurement of US energy, technology and agricultural products
India aims to remove barriers for US agricultural exports such as cotton and nuts

subtopics.title: US Congress and India-US Relations
subtopics.summary: The US Congress is a bicameral legislature, and the Supreme Court ruling makes Congressional approval necessary for broad tariffs. India-US total trade reached USD 129.2 billion in 2024, with India's exports to the US larger than its imports from the US. The US is India's third largest investor.
facts: US Congress is bicameral: House of Representatives and Senate
House has 435 seats; members are elected for 2 years
Senate has 100 seats; every state has 2 seats
Senators are elected for 6 years; one-third of Senate seats are up every 2 years
Republican Party has secured 54 Senate seats
India-US total trade in 2024: USD 129.2 billion
India's exports to US in 2024: USD 87.4 billion
India's imports from US in 2024: USD 41.8 billion
USA is India's 3rd largest investor, with FDI inflows of USD 65.19 billion (2000-2024)

quizzes.passage: The Supreme Court of the United States has struck down a set of tariffs that President Donald Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, commonly called IEEPA. The Court's decision was a 6-3 verdict. Chief Justice John Roberts clarified that IEEPA does not allow a President to take unilateral tariff actions without approval from Congress. In his reasoning, the word 'regulate' in IEEPA does not mean 'tax'. The Court observed that IEEPA was designed for emergency economic restrictions, not for general tariff policy. The Court's reasoning focused on the text and purpose of the statute itself. As a result, the Liberation Day tariffs, introduced through an executive order dated 2 April 2025, were invalidated. Before this order, no American President had used IEEPA as a means to impose trade tariffs. The judgment has also raised questions about whether tariffs already collected can be refunded. It has further raised questions about the direction of future American trade policy. Indian exporters are among those affected, since the Liberation Day tariffs had applied to many of their goods. Any broad tariff measure now needs authorisation from Congress, which places a limit on the use of emergency powers for trade protectionism. This is why the verdict is widely discussed in the context of future trade policy.

quizzes.passage: After the Supreme Court limited the use of emergency economic powers for tariffs, the government had to look to other statutes. The Trade Act of 1974 contains a provision that lets the President impose temporary tariffs. Its purpose is to protect domestic industries and to address trade imbalances or unfair trade practices. The President has used this power to impose a temporary tariff on goods from all countries. A separate provision of the same Act allows action against foreign regulations that unfairly burden American trade. Another route is the Tariff Act of 1930, which permits import tariffs against countries with discriminatory trade practices. The Trade Expansion Act of 1962 allows import restrictions on goods that threaten national security, and this power has been applied to steel and aluminium. Taken together, these laws show that tariff policy can be pursued through specific statutes rather than through emergency powers. Each of these laws addresses a different kind of trade problem, such as a trade imbalance, a threat to national security, unfair foreign regulations or discriminatory trade practices. The government's options therefore depended on matching the legal tool to the specific concern. After the ruling, officials had to choose among these statutes while keeping within the conditions that each one sets out in its own text.
